User-scope, no root; `install-desktop --remove` deletes it (also swept by `uninstall`). The installer offers this on a first install only. | | `connect [args…]` | Authenticate a provider (`opencode auth login`) — agent-free, firewall off. `connect ` asks just for the key of a provider your config declares; `connect --custom [id]` declares a self-hosted endpoint first. | | `mcp-auth ` | Authenticate a remote MCP server's OAuth; the browser callback is forwarded into the sandbox. | | `code [--shell] [--no-nested] [--kvm] [--session ] [args…]` | *Preview.* Run Claude Code on a clone of a forge repo, with open internet but no access to your machine — see [Coding agents](#coding-agents-konrad-code). | | `code up [--no-nested] [--kvm] [--capacity ] ` / `code down ` / `code ls` | *Preview.* Keep a repo up in the background for sessions you start from the Claude app or claude.ai/code; stop it; list the repos that are up. | | `org add` / `list` / `sync` / `remove` | Manage org config-layer subscriptions — see [For organizations](#for-organizations). | | `update` | Refresh the CLI itself, pull the latest image from `ghcr.io/jlbauss/konrad:latest`, and re-sync subscribed org layers. | | `reset` | Wipe shared volumes + log dir. If the launcher is ever clicked on a machine where the `konrad` CLI is missing, it offers to install it first. The `curl | sh` installer offers to create it **on a first install only** — never again on an update, since `konrad update` re-runs that same installer. If you already have a launcher, an update quietly re-generates it in place (the wrapper and the macOS bundle are generated code, so fixes have to reach launchers already on disk) and keeps your settings; if you declined, or removed it, an update leaves you alone and you can add one later with `konrad install-desktop`. `KONRAD_DESKTOP=1` opts in non-interactively at any time, `0` never asks. # Example org layer (git-native)

A starter for the konrad **org config layer** — the layer that lets an
organization ship defaults every user inherits (merged `baked < org < user`).
Publish an adapted copy of this directory as a git repository on your forge;
each member then subscribes once:

```sh
konrad org add https://git.example.com/acme/konrad-org
```

That clones the repo to `~/.config/konrad/org/<name>/`, and every
`konrad update` (or `konrad org sync`) re-syncs it — the layer is a **managed
mirror** that tracks your branch, so shipping an update to the fleet is just
`git push`. Private repos need no konrad-side auth: the member's existing git
credentials (a forge CLI login such as `gh`/`glab auth login`, or SSH) apply.

See [README → Configuration → "For organizations"](../../README.md#for-organizations)
for the user-facing overview and [ARCHITECTURE.md → Configuration & instructions](../../ARCHITECTURE.md#configuration--instructions)
for the *why*.

## What's here

```text
org-package/                 Publish this as a git repo — the repo IS the layer.
├── opencode.jsonc           Org-wide config: an internal provider + a declared model.
├── instructions/            Org instructions — every *.md here loads on the system channel.
│   └── house-rules.md
├── skills/
│   └── house-style/
│       └── SKILL.md         A trivial example house skill.
└── hooks/
    └── post-sync            Optional. Runs host-side after add + every sync (see below).
```

The layer holds the same optional pieces as a user's `~/.config/konrad/user/`
(`opencode.jsonc`, `agents/`, `skills/`, `instructions/`, `AGENTS.md`,
`fonts/`, `allowed_hosts`); this example populates three plus a hook. Ship only
what your org needs. Several orgs can coexist as sibling layers — they fold in
alphabetical name order (pick precedence with a numeric prefix: `10-core`,
`20-team`), each still below every user's own layer.

## The post-sync hook (trust boundary)

`hooks/post-sync`, when present and executable, runs **on the member's machine**
after the initial `konrad org add` and after every successful sync — the one
place org code runs outside konrad's sandbox. Subscribing to a layer *is* the
decision to trust its code; konrad adds no prompt. Use it for the few jobs plain
config can't express — mirroring a wiki into `~/.config/konrad/context/` for the
agent to grep, or deriving per-member identity from your forge's CLI — and keep
it idempotent: it runs on every sync, changed or not. The example hook just
stamps a marker file so you can watch the mechanism; replace or delete it.

Because the dominant sync path is now the **unwatched** background refresh, a
hook's `echo` no longer reaches a human. konrad exports `KONRAD_NOTICE_DIR` (plus
`KONRAD_LAYER_NAME` and `KONRAD_HOOK_INTERACTIVE`) so the hook can drop a
`key: value` notice — `severity: info|warn|blocked`, `summary:`, optional
`detail:`/`fix:` — that konrad renders (attributed to your layer, sanitized) at
the member's next launch. The example hook sketches the high-value case: telling
a member, in your own words, when their forge sign-in has expired and frozen the
mirror. See [ARCHITECTURE.md → Distribution & updates](../../ARCHITECTURE.md#distribution--updates).

## Adapt it

- **`opencode.jsonc`** — point `baseURL` at your real internal gateway, declare
  the models you've actually deployed, add any provider keys via opencode's
  `{env:VAR}` placeholders. This merges *under* each user's
  `user/opencode.jsonc`, so a user can still override or add on top.
- **`instructions/*.md`** — your house rules. Every `.md` here loads additively
  on the system instructions channel (precedence: konrad's `environment.md` →
  **org** → user `AGENTS.md` → project `AGENTS.md`). Split rules across files,
  or have the hook generate one. (A single `AGENTS.md` at the layer root still
  works as a back-compat alias.)
- **`skills/`**, **`agents/`**, **`fonts/`**, **`allowed_hosts`** — house
  skills, house agents, corporate fonts, extra egress-firewall hosts. Same
  layering: org sits between baked and user.

## Note: defaults, not enforcement

Everything here lands in the user's own home directory, so a determined user can
edit it (local edits to tracked files are simply clobbered on the next sync).
The org layer is a **defaults** mechanism, not a policy lock — "add-only"
describes the merge precedence (user stacks on top), not a permission boundary.
If you need config a user can't override, this isn't it.

# Do the docx and powerpoint skills make konrad's Word and PowerPoint work better?

*A/B test report · office-skills · 2026-10-28*

**Of 6 tasks, A was better in 2, B in 0, and 4 showed no real difference.**

> **In short.** Two versions of konrad, A (main, without the docx and powerpoint skills) and B (with the docx and powerpoint skills (and the layout repair on the create tasks)), did the same 6 tasks, 10 times each, with the same AI model. Every result was checked automatically for hard facts, and every pair of results was compared by AI reviewers who didn't know which version made which.

## 4. What else the runs showed

- **Time and work per task.** 27B took about six times as long per run (190 s against 32 s) and twice as many steps (19 against 9). Each step re-reads the conversation so far, so it read 2.4 times as many tokens (600k against 250k per run). One 27B run hit the 15-minute limit, on xlsx-create-report, after delivering a correct workbook.
- **Cost.** opencode's estimate for the 85 runs per side: $0.62 for Haiku and $2.15 for 27B. OpenRouter's bill for 27B came to about $5.50, because opencode prices every call at the cheapest provider OpenRouter lists, while the account's routing settings sent the calls to costlier ones. At the bill's prices, a 27B run cost about nine times a Haiku run here.
- **Language.** On the German board minutes, 27B wrote its table in English in all five runs; Haiku kept to German. 27B also listed the rejected proposals in a second table in all five runs, where the request said to leave them out.
- **Where 27B won:** the budget edit, five pairs of five. Haiku's chart lost the new Marketing row every time, because its range wasn't extended (the openpyxl pitfall the first skills test also found). 27B extended it.
- **Tool calls.** None failed on either side. Once in 85 runs (xlsx-edit-budget, run 1), 27B's reply carried a stray `</invoke>` tag and its own notes on earlier steps; the run still finished and won its pair.

## 5. Limits

- 5 pairs per task show clear differences, not subtle ones.
- The reviewers are AI models. They agreed with themselves as shown above, but nobody checked every verdict by hand.
- Each model ran at the effort shown, through one provider; the same model served elsewhere (another provider, a local runtime, a quantized build) may behave differently.
- The reviewers are kept blind by instruction: they could have looked at other files on disk.
- **The letter task had a mistake.** Its notes say a three-month notice to 31 December still works on 29 October, which it doesn't. One Haiku run noticed and asked instead of writing the letter; it counts as a loss, and the task is corrected after this run.
- **The contract task's win is thin.** The documents were identical; the reviewers preferred Haiku because 27B named the client as the author of its review comment.
- **The reviewers' blindness slipped in four of 34 batches:** a wildcard in a shell command read files in other packets (an input file in two cases, other verdicts after writing their own in two). X and Y are drawn at random per packet, so none of it tells a reviewer which model is which. One reviewer judged three spreadsheet packets from their text and structure without the page images, and spreadsheets' frozen panes don't show in a packet at all.

Both versions ran with `openrouter/qwen/qwen3.8-27b (default effort)`. Each request ended with: “If one of your skills covers this file type, load it with the skill tool before you start, and follow it.” The tasks:

- **docx-edit-contract**: “Our client Nordlicht GmbH is now called Polarstern AG.”
- **pptx-create-deck**: “Make a 16:9 deck quarterly-review.pptx for Friday's sales meeting, five slides in this order.”

## 2. How

1. **Same task, same input, 5 runs per version.** Run 1 of No skills and run 1 of Skills form a *pair*, and so on.
1. **Automatic checks.** Each task has a small test that checks fixed facts about the result (is the old name gone, is the chart there). They tell whether a result is correct, not whether it is good.
1. **Blind review.** An AI reviewer (Opus, as the ab-judge agent) gets the request, the input and both results as page images and text, labelled only “X” and “Y” in random order. It scores both on *request* (did it do what was asked), *fidelity* (is the data right) and *presentation* (could you hand it on as it is), and says which it would rather receive, or that it makes no difference.
1. **Each pair is reviewed twice,** by different reviewers, with X and Y swapped. A pair counts as a win only if both reviews pick the same version, otherwise as no difference. Here they agreed in 32 of 35 pairs.
1. **A task's outcome** is “clearly better” when one version wins at least half of all pairs more than the other, “somewhat better” when it wins at least two more, and “no real difference” otherwise.

## 4. Limits

- 10 pairs per task show clear differences, not subtle ones.
- The reviewers are AI models. They agreed with themselves as shown above, but nobody checked every verdict by hand.
- The runs used `anthropic/claude-haiku-5-5 (low effort)`; another model, such as the local one konrad is tuned for, may behave differently.
- Each reviewer could open only its own batch's folder, so the other packets and the runs' files stayed out of its reach.
- The two xlsx reports of 2026-10-29 ran the xlsx side separately, ten times each, so their xlsx numbers differ by the spread between runs (the chart in xlsx-edit-budget kept its range in 2 of 10 runs in one and 5 of 10 in the other).
- The page renders don't show frozen panes, so the reviewers couldn't judge the frozen header in xlsx-create-report; the automatic checks cover it.
- The prompt suffix made Haiku load the skill in every run, so this measures the skill's content, not what a user sees: unprompted, Haiku loads a spreadsheet skill in 0–2 of 10 runs, while Qwen3.8 27B loads it every time ([models report](../2026-10-29-models/)).

# Architecture

How konrad is built and *why* — the load-bearing choices and the rationale behind the non-obvious ones. Where this doc and the code disagree, the code is canonical; fix the doc.

## Repository guide

One audience and one job per file:

| File | Purpose |
| --- | --- |
| [README.md](README.md) | End-user guide — what konrad is, install, use, configure. |
| [ARCHITECTURE.md](ARCHITECTURE.md) | This file — system design and the *why*. |
| [CONTRIBUTING.md](CONTRIBUTING.md) | Contributor guide — dev loop, branching, commit style, **versioning & releases**. |
| [CLAUDE.md](CLAUDE.md) | Instructions for AI agents working on konrad's source. |
| [ROADMAP.md](ROADMAP.md) | Backlog: at most ten items, what to delete when it gets in the way, and the upstream bugs konrad works around or lives with. |
| [CHANGELOG.md](CHANGELOG.md) | Released, user-facing changes (Keep a Changelog), written by CI from the commits at each release ([cliff.toml](cliff.toml)). |
| [SECURITY.md](SECURITY.md) | How to report a vulnerability, and what counts as one. |
| [VERSION](VERSION) | Single source of the version; drives image tags. |

Code layout (`bin/`, `image/`, `scripts/`) is mapped in [CONTRIBUTING.md](CONTRIBUTING.md#repo-layout--what-goes-where).

## The big picture

konrad runs [opencode](https://github.com/sst/opencode) inside a sandboxed, rootless Podman container.

- **The image is the canonical artifact.** `image/Dockerfile` builds it; `bin/konrad` — a thin host-side bash CLI — is the primary consumer.
- **No IDE attaches to the sandbox — deliberately.** VS Code Dev Containers bridges every attached container to the host through sockets in `/tmp`: the host's `git credential` helper, the SSH agent, askpass, and the IPC channel, over which code in the container can install an extension that types commands into a *host* terminal. Microsoft treats this as by design, and no setting closes all of it, so attaching would carry a host channel *inside* the firewall boundary and void "can't touch anything outside the workspace."
- **Podman, not Docker.** Open-source, free for commercial use, ergonomic on macOS. `--userns=keep-id` shares the container `node` user's UID with the host user, so bind-mounted files have sane ownership. Docker isn't supported.
- **Two engines, one abstraction.** The supported platforms are Linux with Podman and Apple-Silicon macOS 26+ with Apple's [`container`](https://github.com/apple/container), which konrad always picks on macOS; there's no Podman fallback for other Macs, because testing every change on a third platform costs more than those Macs are worth. The two CLIs aren't subcommand-compatible, so every host-side engine call in `bin/konrad` goes through an `eng_*` wrapper and `detect_engine()` fixes the choice once at startup (`KONRAD_ENGINE` overrides). apple/container needs no `--userns` (VirtioFS maps guest UIDs → the host user) and rejects the `:z`/`:U`/`:ro` mount suffixes, so those are dropped there. Its named volumes are root-owned and can't be chowned, so the three persistent stores (secrets/cache/state) are host directories under `~/.local/state/konrad/store/`, which VirtioFS remaps to the container user like the `/workspace` bind. The remap is per lookup: VirtioFS reports a file as owned by whichever guest uid asked, briefly cached, so an ownership check can see root or a nested container's uid on a file node owns. Block-backed volumes would give real ownership but attach to one VM at a time, and `konrad code`'s config, tools and clone are shared across sessions and repos, so they stay on VirtioFS and the ownership-checking tools stand down instead: `konrad code` trusts the clone as a git `safe.directory` and sets `XDG_CONFIG_HOME` to its default, which podman then doesn't second-guess.
- **A wedged engine fails fast, not forever.** Short apple/container calls (status, network create and delete, container removal and the teardown) and org post-sync hooks run under `bounded`, the one shell watchdog in [bin/konrad](bin/konrad) (stock macOS has no GNU `timeout`); interactive runs don't, since they're meant to last. The case that made it necessary: apple/container's service keeps running from the install it started from, so after `brew upgrade container` deletes that install, every network and container start blocks. `container_service_check` reads `container system status` before a launch (server version ≠ client version, or the install root gone) and stops with the fix. It doesn't restart the service itself: a restart ends every running container, other konrad sessions and `konrad code up` repos included, and the fix is one command after an upgrade.
- **Tuned for Qwen3.6-class local models.** The agent prompt ([image/opencode/agents/konrad.md](image/opencode/agents/konrad.md)) is sized for a ~30B-class local model; the tested recommendation is `qwen/qwen3.6-27b`. Frontier models work fine; sub-10B ones may need prompt softening.

## Engineering ethos — lightweight, composed, low-maintenance

The guiding principle behind every other choice here: **konrad stays lightweight and leans on well-maintained building blocks rather than custom code.** Prefer configuring an existing tool over shipping bespoke machinery; drive ongoing maintenance toward zero, so konrad keeps working and current even through stretches when no one is actively developing it. (This is why model-discovery's custom plugin was dropped, the config deep-merge is a tiny self-contained step, and the whole pinning/rebuild story is a bot plus upstream registries.)

Its second face: **simple, logical, and smooth beats clever.** konrad should stay tidy and resist sprawl. A solution that *feels* surprising (e.g. the runtime user lacking write access everywhere in its own home) is a smell to fix at the structural cause, not a quirk to live with — today's quiet workaround is tomorrow's unexpected consequence. Accumulating complexity is debt to pay down deliberately; periodic cleanliness passes are part of the maintenance story.

## Configuration & instructions

Config is **layered, not replaced** — host-mergeable layers, folded left, last writer wins:

```text
baked image defaults   <   org layers (0..n)             <   user
/etc/konrad/…               ~/.config/konrad/org/<name>/      ~/.config/konrad/user/
```

- Each layer holds the same opencode pieces — `opencode.jsonc`, `agents/`, `skills/`, `instructions/`, `AGENTS.md`, `fonts/`. [image/entrypoint.sh](image/entrypoint.sh) composes the `opencode.jsonc` of each via [image/merge-config.js](image/merge-config.js) (an N-input deep-merge) before opencode loads anything. **Objects merge recursively; arrays replace** — which is why agent rules are added via `AGENTS.md` or `instructions/`, not by overriding the `instructions` array. (A layer may also carry an `allowed_hosts` file — konrad-specific, consumed by the egress firewall, *not* part of this merge.)
- **`org/` is a container of named layers, and a subscribed layer is a managed git mirror.** `konrad org add <git-url>` clones a repo to `org/<name>/`; `konrad org sync` (riding every `konrad update`) does `git fetch` + `reset --hard @{u}`. Local edits to tracked files are clobbered by design (the user's channel is `user/`, which always merges on top); a failed sync warns and keeps the last-good checkout (availability beats freshness for a defaults mechanism); and there's **no state file**, since the in-place `.git` records URL and branch. Layers fold in alphabetical name order (`10-`/`20-` prefixes steer precedence); a plain non-git dir is a manual layer that never syncs; a detached-HEAD checkout (a tag) is the pin. So an org ships updates by `git push`, with no bespoke updater and **no konrad auth code**: private repos work through the member's existing git credentials. The entrypoint, [compose-allowed-hosts.sh](image/konrad-defaults/compose-allowed-hosts.sh) and the overlay loops all walk the *same* sorted enumeration, so precedence can't drift between channels, and the firewall derivation sees **every** layer's providers (a missed layer would silently block that org's internal endpoint).
- **The `hooks/post-sync` hook is a deliberate exception to "agent code runs only in the sandbox."** A layer may ship an executable `hooks/post-sync`; konrad runs it host-side after `add` and after every successful sync (cwd = the layer dir). It covers the org needs plain config can't express (mirror a corpus into `context/`, derive per-member identity from the org's own forge auth), and it *rides the branch*, so it updates with the layer. Trust model: **subscribing is trusting** — no prompt, no flag; adding a layer is the decision to run its code. konrad gains no declarative corpus-sync engine.
  - **The hook environment is a small contract,** because the usual sync path is the unwatched background worker, where `echo` reaches no one. konrad exports `KONRAD_NOTICE_DIR` (where to drop notices, the layer's channel to its members; see [below](#distribution--updates)), `KONRAD_LAYER_NAME`, and `KONRAD_HOOK_INTERACTIVE` (`1` on `add`/`sync`/`update`, `0` under the worker, so a hook picks `echo` vs. a notice without sniffing the tty). The hook is time-bounded (`KONRAD_HOOK_TIMEOUT`, default 120 s, under `bounded`) so an unwatched hang can't live until reboot.
- **Discovery is a well-known `$HOME` folder** (`~/.config/konrad/{org,user}`), not an env var or system path — because apple/container's VirtioFS remap makes paths under `$HOME` readable as the container user, and a user-level default needs no root to install.
- **Every read-only host bind is relabelled on Podman (`ro_bind`: `:ro,z`).** A dir under `~/.config` keeps its home label (`config_home_t`) through a plain bind, and no container type may search it, so on an SELinux host the org, user, `context/` and code layers would be mounted but unreadable, and the entrypoints, which only take what `[[ -f ]]`/`[[ -d ]]` finds, would run without them. *Shared* (`z`), not private (`Z`): the agent, the firewall sidecar, `konrad code up` and parallel sessions bind the same dirs at once, each with its own MCS pair, and a private label would lock out all but the last. The content is meant for the agent anyway, so a label every container can read adds no exposure. Both entrypoints warn when a bound layer is unreadable.
- **`AGENTS.md` is the user's slot; `instructions` is konrad's.** opencode loads both, additively. The baked `opencode.jsonc` declares one glob for the baked `instructions/` dir and one for the user's, and opencode expands them itself (skipping absent paths, de-duplicating, preserving order). **Org layers can't get a glob of their own**: opencode globs only an entry's *basename* (the dirname is literal), so `org/*/instructions/*.md` could never match. Instead the entrypoint **copies** each layer's `instructions/*.md` (and a layer-root `AGENTS.md`) into the baked `instructions/` dir as `org-<name>-<file>`, where the baked glob finds them — the same mechanism as the generated allow-list file, and the array-replace footgun never bites because only the baked layer declares the `instructions` array. Precedence, all additive: `environment.md → org instructions → user instructions → user AGENTS.md → project AGENTS.md`.
- The org layer is **defaults, not enforcement**: files in the user's own home, so "add-only" describes merge precedence, not a permission lock.
- **Model discovery is an inline entrypoint probe, and there's no baked `model`.** Provider endpoints ship pre-wired with empty model lists; at session start [discover-models.sh](image/konrad-defaults/discover-models.sh) probes `<baseURL>/models` for every provider with an explicit `options.baseURL`, in parallel and bounded (`KONRAD_DISCOVERY_TIMEOUT`; `KONRAD_NO_DISCOVERY=1` opts out), drops embedding models, and merges the results *below* the composed config, so discovery fills the picker but a declared model still wins. Each model gets `limit.context` when the endpoint exposes a window (vLLM's `max_model_len`, llama.cpp's `meta.n_ctx`), because opencode's auto-compaction keys off it; the probe never *guesses* a window, since a wrong one mis-compacts. opencode requires both `limit` keys once the object exists, so a discovered `context` gets a derived `limit.output` of `context/6` (floor 2048, capped at the window): proportional, because opencode subtracts it from the context to size compaction *and* sends it as `max_tokens`. The probe runs as `node` in the sandbox and sends each provider key only to the endpoint opencode itself would call, **through the firewall proxy**, so the key invariant holds and authenticated remote endpoints are discovered too. It replaced an upstream discovery plugin that cost seconds per start and a fragile build-time dependency. When opencode gains native `/models` discovery ([opencode#27554](https://github.com/anomalyco/opencode/pull/27554)), the probe can go.
- **Tool permissions are sandbox-shaped and live once, globally.** The baseline `permission` block sits in [opencode-defaults.jsonc](image/konrad-defaults/opencode-defaults.jsonc) (top-level, so every agent inherits it); per-agent blocks carry **only deltas**. The model follows the boundary, not the action's scariness: the container is disposable and non-root, so the agent acts freely *inside* it (`allow`), `ask` is reserved for the one irreversible action on the user's real files (`rm -rf` in the `/workspace` bind), and `deny` covers the escape vectors — root (`sudo`), host container/cluster control (`podman`/`docker`/`kubectl`), and the secrets volume under `external_directory`. Network tools stay `allow` because the [egress firewall](#egress-firewall) is the real network boundary. Only `ask` interrupts, so prompts are rare by design. opencode applies the *last* matching rule, so each object lists its catch-all first and the exceptions after it, and a layer's added rule lands last and wins; smoke-test.sh proves the denies by calling the tools, which also catches an opencode release that renames a key. Subagents add `question: deny` (no user in their loop) and tighten `rm -rf` to `deny`; [manual-transformer](image/opencode/agents/manual-transformer.md) is the worked example.

## State, secrets & isolation

**`.agent/` belongs to the agent end-to-end; framework state lives elsewhere.**

```text
.agent/
  task.md                     # planning artifact (committable)
  artifacts/                  # durable mid-task outputs (committable)
  scratch/                    # agent scripts / probes
  quality-assurance/<stamp>/  # verification evidence on a fail
```

- **konrad doesn't touch the workspace at startup.** It neither creates the `.agent/` tree (the agent and the quality-assurance helper `mkdir -p` their own dirs on demand), nor prunes it, nor edits `.gitignore`, nor writes a session sidecar. A launch leaves a clean repo clean.
- **A no-project launch gets an ephemeral scratch workspace, not a refusal.** `$HOME` can't be the workspace — it hands the agent the whole home, and SELinux hosts refuse the bind outright. So `konrad scratch` (and the bare `konrad` TUI launched from `$HOME`) mints a fresh timestamped dir under `~/.local/state/konrad/scratch/<stamp>/` and binds *that*. It **must sit under `$HOME`**, where apple/container's VirtioFS remap applies (a host `/tmp` dir wouldn't be writable), and in konrad's own state dir it's swept by the retention prune and wiped by `konrad reset`. konrad creates only the empty dir, so "doesn't touch the workspace" still holds. `shell`/`run` keep the hard refusal (an automation path shouldn't silently invent a directory). `konrad open` reveals the newest scratch dir in the host file manager.
- **Retention is one shared window.** The log dir and the scratch workspaces are both pruned at launch by age (`KONRAD_RETENTION_DAYS`, default 30; `0` disables). The scratch prune deletes *agent-written content*, which is why the off switch exists and why the prune runs *before* a fresh scratch dir is minted.
- **Sessions are ephemeral.** opencode's `~/.local/share/opencode/` isn't bind-mounted — sessions, S

A swap is judged on behaviour, not on reading: [scripts/ab-test.sh](scripts/ab-test.sh) runs the old and the new image on the same graded tasks with a real model.
- The Python venv ships as **three `COPY` layers** (the `venv-split` build stage partitions it): torch (~700 MB), the large slow-moving numeric wheels (opencv/scipy/numpy/onnxruntime/sympy, ~450 MB), and the churny remainder (~360 MB). So the near-daily `python.lock` bump of a small pure-python dep re-pulls just the light layer, while torch and the numeric set dedupe.
- The GitLab `resolve-locks` bot re-resolves each upstream daily and opens an auto-merging MR **only when something moved**, so a rebuild fires only when there's something new; no scheduled rebuild. `main` takes no direct pushes, the bot's included (protected branch; *Pipelines must succeed*), so every commit on it passed `check` in an MR pipeline. Freshness is a bot plus upstream registries, not hand-tended bumps.
- **Reproducible layers** — CI builds with `SOURCE_DATE_EPOCH=0` + `rewrite-timestamp=true`, so byte-identical content yields byte-identical layer digests and users skip a re-download when nothing changed. Local `konrad-dev rebuild` writes `konrad:local`, separate from the published `:latest`.
- **CI runs on a GitHub mirror; the primary repo stays on `gitlab.git.nrw`** (one-way push mirror → GitHub Actions does build → smoke → publish to `ghcr.io/jlbauss/konrad`), because the image build needs privileged runners. gitlab.git.nrw has since turned out to offer them, so the build could move back and the mirror go (design and probes in the [ROADMAP history](https://gitlab.git.nrw/jbauss2/konrad/-/blob/7c4aaca0b01804e465d7980a3463674c9347996f/ROADMAP.md), *Collapse the two-forge setup*). The GitHub side takes no contributions — CI plus auto-mirrored releases only. (Contributor and release flow: [CONTRIBUTING.md](CONTRIBUTING.md).)

## Distribution & updates

**konrad ships as two artifacts that version and update on independent channels.** The **CLI** (`bin/konrad`, a bash script) and the **image** (the canonical artifact, pulled from GHCR) drift by design — a CLI-only patch bumps `VERSION` without firing an image rebuild (the workflow's `image/**` paths filter), so `konrad --version` prints both.

- **The CLI updates through its install channel,** `curl|sh`. konrad never self-updates the CLI from a *background* process — rewriting the running script mid-flight is a footgun, and the install channel owns the binary. `konrad update` on a `curl|sh` install re-runs the installer, which fetches from `main`; a symlink (dev) install is left to `git pull`.
- **The image (and org layers) stay fresh via a throttled background refresh** — the piece an install channel can't provide for a ~1 GB GHCR image. Every launching verb calls `maybe_background_refresh` ([bin/konrad](bin/konrad)): at most once per `KONRAD_REFRESH_INTERVAL` (default daily), it fires a **detached** worker that pulls `:latest`, re-tags the local `konrad:latest`, and runs `org_sync_all`. The launch never waits on it and never fails because of it; the *next* launch picks up a newer image, announced in one line only when the pulled image's **content ID** changed.
- **Availability beats freshness.** The throttle stamp is written *before* the worker runs, so a failed or slow refresh still counts against the interval rather than retrying every launch, like an org sync keeping its last-good checkout. `konrad update` does the same refresh **synchronously and now**, plus the CLI. Worker output goes to `~/.local/state/konrad/refresh.log`, never the terminal.
- **The notice queue carries news from unwatched work to the next launch.** Org sync rides the background worker, so a layer's `post-sync` hook fires detached, its output going to the refresh log. The worker or a hook (via `KONRAD_NOTICE_DIR`) writes one `key: value` file per notice under `~/.local/state/konrad/notices/`; `launch_preflight` renders and deletes them (`notices_flush` in [bin/konrad](bin/konrad)). Each choice is load-bearing:
  - **Stateless:** a notice is rendered then dropped, and the next refresh re-creates it while the fault persists, so a fixed fault's notice disappears with nothing to acknowledge or migrate.
  - **Source by path, not by field:** a top-level file is `konrad`'s, an `org-<name>/` subdir is that layer's, so a hook can't forge konrad-branded text (its lines are sanitized and capped on render).
  - **A severity ladder that never breaks the launch:** `info` is one dim line, `warn` a framed block, `blocked` adds an Enter-to-continue *only* on an interactive stdin (never under a piped `konrad run`, `KONRAD_NO_NOTICES=1`, or a disabled refresh).
  - A non-zero hook that wrote no notice has its last output lines promoted into a `warn` attributed to the layer, so existing layers gain visibility with no change on their side.

**The desktop launcher is generated on-machine, not shipped.** `konrad install-desktop` writes a user-scope launcher (a freedesktop `.desktop` + hicolor icon on Linux; a `~/Applications/Konrad.app` bundle on macOS) whose action is `konrad scratch`, since a GUI launch has no project cwd and lands in the [ephemeral scratch workspace](#state-secrets--isolation).

- **One shared wrapper script** (`~/.local/share/konrad/launch.sh`) locates konrad (a GUI `PATH` often omits `~/.local/bin`), offers to `curl|sh`-install it if missing, then execs `konrad scratch`, so the behaviour lives in one place.
- **The TUI needs a terminal a GUI click doesn't provide.** Linux leans on `.desktop` `Terminal=true` (DE-dependent; `install-desktop` warns when no terminal launcher is found); the macOS bundle spawns one around the wrapper (Terminal.app by default; `KONRAD_TERMINAL` picks `ghostty`/`alacritty`/`iterm`, validated against LaunchServices at install, since macOS has no default-terminal setting).
- **One icon source:** the committed [`assets/konrad.svg`](assets/konrad.svg), installed verbatim on Linux and rasterized (via the committed PNG master and the preinstalled `sips`/`iconutil`) into the mac `.icns`; a `curl|sh` install fetches it from the repo (offline → generic icon, the launcher still works).
- **Regenerating is ask-free and choice-preserving,** because `konrad update` re-runs the installer, so the launcher step runs on every update. The opt-in question is asked only on a genuinely fresh install (the installer already knows, from its clobber check); a decline stands, with `konrad install-desktop` as the opt-in later. An upgrade runs `install-desktop --refresh`, which regenerates **only an existing launcher**, so wrapper fixes reach launchers on disk without creating one the user declined. The terminal choice is stored **in the launcher itself** (a `TERM_ID` line that `resolve_mac_terminal` reads back when `KONRAD_TERMINAL` is unset), so there's no state to write, migrate or leave behind; a recorded value that's no longer supported warns and falls back. Both back-ends build the icon into a temp and move it in only on success, so an offline refresh never downgrades a working launcher.

This is host-side GUI integration only — no sandbox, engine, or image involvement, like `konrad open`.

**AGPL-3.0** — compatible with all bundled upstream licenses (MIT, Apache-2.0, OFL-1.1). Strong copyleft is deliberate for a sandbox-style tool: AGPL's network-use clause closes the SaaS loophole plain GPL leaves open, so a fork offered as a hosted remote agent over an API must still publish its source. - **The Podman fallback on macOS.** On a Mac konrad now always uses Apple's `container` (Apple silicon, macOS 26+), and says so when it's missing, instead of falling back to Podman in a `podman machine` VM, which was untested and unsupported.

- **Image builds no longer fill the disk.** `konrad-dev rebuild` removes the images a rebuild replaced and the leftovers of interrupted builds, and tags its last intermediate stage (`konrad-venv-split:cache`) so it stays cached. Each nested `konrad code` session start removes dangling images and leftover build containers older than a day from the repo's image store, which had no limit.

See [README → Troubleshooting](README.md#troubleshooting).
- Short engine calls on Apple's `container` (status, network create and delete, container removal, the cleanup when a session ends) give up after `KONRAD_ENGINE_TIMEOUT` seconds (default 30) instead of hanging; they were unbounded on a Mac without GNU `timeout`.

### Fixed

- **The desktop-launcher question is asked once, on a first install — not on every update.** `konrad update` re-runs the installer, which had no notion of "already installed", so it re-offered the launcher every single time. The offer is now gated on a genuinely fresh install; an update never asks. Declining stays declined (add one later with `konrad install-desktop`), and `KONRAD_DESKTOP=1`/`0` still force the answer at any time.
- **Your macOS terminal choice now sticks.** `KONRAD_TERMINAL` only ever existed as an install-time variable, so any regeneration without it — clicking through an update, or just re-running `konrad install-desktop` — silently reset a Ghostty/Alacritty/iTerm launcher back to Terminal.app. The launcher now records its own choice and keeps it; pass `KONRAD_TERMINAL` again only when you want to change it. Launchers created by earlier versions are recognised too, so upgrading doesn't reset yours on the way in. A recorded terminal that's since been uninstalled warns and falls back instead of failing the run.
- **An update keeps an existing launcher current instead of leaving it stale.** The wrapper script and the macOS bundle are generated, so fixes to them now reach launchers already on disk via the new `konrad install-desktop --refresh` — which regenerates only what's already installed and is a silent no-op otherwise. A refresh can no longer *downgrade* a working launcher either: an offline icon fetch keeps the installed icon rather than replacing it with a generic one.

# Contributing to konrad

Thanks for your interest. konrad is an in-house tool, developed in the open ([README → Status](README.md#status)): one person maintains it for their own and their team's use, so issues and merge requests are welcome but come with no promise of review or response time. Small, focused changes stand the best chance.

## Before you start

If you're proposing something larger than a typo fix, **open a GitLab issue first** to discuss. A short "I'd like to add X — does that fit?" conversation saves rework when the maintainer would have steered you elsewhere. For tiny things (typos, broken links, obvious one-line bugs), skip straight to a merge request.

What "larger" means in practice:

- A new bundled skill or agent
- A new CLI subcommand or flag
- Any change to config layering, state isolation, or the entrypoint
- Any non-trivial Dockerfile change

What does *not* need an issue first:

- Documentation fixes
- Tightening shellcheck cleanliness
- Adding a missing case to the smoke test
- Floating-pin maintenance (the daily CI normally handles this, but manual PRs are welcome too)

## What you're agreeing to

By submitting a merge request you agree your contributions are licensed under **AGPL-3.0-or-later** (see [LICENSE](LICENSE)). konrad is strong-copyleft on purpose — anyone running it (including over a network) has to publish their source. If that's incompatible with your situation, please don't submit.

No CLA, no DCO. The license terms attach automatically.

Licensing follows the [REUSE](https://reuse.software) spec, verified by `reuse lint`. **Add an SPDX header to every new or edited source file** — two comment lines near the top:

```text
# SPDX-FileCopyrightText: 2026 Your Name
# SPDX-License-Identifier: AGPL-3.0-or-later
```

Vendored third-party files keep their *upstream* `SPDX-FileCopyrightText` + license instead. Files that can't carry a comment (fonts, other binaries) and the project default are handled by globs in [`REUSE.toml`](REUSE.toml); when you introduce a new license, add its text under `LICENSES/` (`reuse download <SPDX-ID>`). Keep `reuse lint` green — CI enforces it.

## First-time setup

konrad keeps the user CLI and the dev CLI as separate binaries on `PATH`, so you can hack on the source without disturbing your day-to-day stable `konrad`:

| Binary       | Source of CLI                  | Default image  | Refresh with                |
| ------------ | ------------------------------ | -------------- | --------------------------- |
| `konrad`     | Standalone install (curl\|sh)  | `konrad:latest` | `konrad update`          |
| `konrad-dev` | Symlink to your checkout       | `konrad:local`  | `konrad-dev rebuild`     |

Same script under the hood — `bin/konrad` picks its default image from `basename "$0"`. The two never collide, and you only need both if you want a stable agent alongside an in-flight dev build.

```sh
# 1. The user CLI (skip if you already have it).
curl -fsSL https://gitlab.git.nrw/jbauss2/konrad/-/raw/main/scripts/install.sh | sh

# 2. The dev CLI.
git clone https://gitlab.git.nrw/jbauss2/konrad.git
cd konrad
mkdir -p ~/.local/bin && ln -sfn "$(pwd)/bin/konrad" ~/.local/bin/konrad-dev

# 3. Build the dev image and smoke-test.
konrad-dev rebuild
./scripts/smoke-test.sh konrad:local
```

You need:

- A container engine — **Podman** on Linux (and inside `konrad code`), or Apple's **`container`** on Apple-Silicon macOS 26+. `konrad-dev rebuild` builds on whichever it runs on: Podman via buildah, apple/container via `container build` (straight into its own store — no Podman needed on the Mac). Docker is on the roadmap but not supported yet.
- `~/.local/bin` on your `$PATH`

- **uv** and **node** (with `npx`) for `scripts/check.sh`, which fetches the lint tools at pinned versions on first use

That's the whole host toolchain; there's deliberately no dev container (why: [ARCHITECTURE → konrad code](ARCHITECTURE.md#konrad-code)). In VS Code, accept the workspace's recommended extensions (markdownlint and shellcheck, both bundling their linter) — [.vscode/settings.json](.vscode/settings.json) applies the markdownlint fixes on save. For a shell with the agent's exact toolset and a nested Podman, nothing installed on your host, run `konrad code --shell https://gitlab.git.nrw/jbauss2/konrad`: the same sealed box an agent works in, with its own clone.

**Agents work in `konrad code`, not in your checkout.** Launch one with `konrad code https://gitlab.git.nrw/jbauss2/konrad`: a disposable container with its own clone, its own rootless Podman (so it builds, smoke-tests and self-tests the image itself) and open internet, but no host mounts and a sealed LAN; it hands work back only as a merge request ([ARCHITECTURE → konrad code](ARCHITECTURE.md#konrad-code)). The agent-side rules live in [CLAUDE.md](CLAUDE.md).

## Local development loop

```sh
# Edit files...
konrad-dev rebuild                                      # builds konrad:local
konrad-dev shell                                        # exercise the dev image
./scripts/check.sh                                        # static gates (what CI runs)
./scripts/smoke-test.sh konrad:local                      # smoke (image artifact)
./scripts/selftest.sh                                     # end-to-end (image + a real run)
```

`konrad-dev` defaults to the `konrad:local` image (the one its own `rebuild` writes), so you exercise your dev build with no env var fiddling. The stable `konrad` next to it on `PATH` keeps pointing at `konrad:latest` — your day-to-day agent work is unaffected by whatever you're testing.

The validation gates are:

- `./scripts/check.sh` — the static gates and the unit tests in one command: `bash -n`, shellcheck, `reuse lint`, markdownlint, actionlint, hadolint, and `tests`, the [bats](https://github.com/bats-core/bats-core) suites in [tests/](tests/) (`bin/konrad`'s host-side functions under the script's own `set -euo pipefail`, and `merge-config.js`'s layering contract), each tool at a version pinned in the script; `tests` also needs `jq`. GitLab CI runs the same script on every MR, so a green local run is a green pipeline. `./scripts/check.sh <gate>…` runs a subset.
- `./scripts/build-image.sh` — does the image build?
- `./scripts/test-autoupdate.sh` — the update rehearsal: installs the previous release's CLI under a throwaway `HOME`, then runs a real `konrad update` and background refresh against a local registry holding `konrad:local` and this checkout's files instead of the forge. Run it after `konrad-dev rebuild` for any change to `bin/konrad`, `scripts/install.sh` or the update path. Podman only (the nested engine in `konrad code` is fine).
- `./scripts/ab-test.sh --a <image> --b <image> <task>…` — for a change whose effect only shows in what the agent does (a skill swapped for an upstream one, a prompt edit): runs each task in [tests/ab/](tests/ab/) several times per image through `konrad-dev run` with a real model, A and B interleaved, grades every run with the task's `grade.py`, and writes a report of score, cost, time, steps and skills loaded under `.skill-eval/`. The runs get a `HOME` of their own: copies of your org and user layers (so your providers work) under a layer that allows `rm -rf`, whose `ask` a `konrad run` can only reject, which ends the run. A task is a `prompt.md`, an `input/` dir and a grader that prints which checks passed; the tasks cover Word, Excel and PowerPoint files, emails, PDFs (reading a table, writing a letter), a receipt photo, a CSV analysis with a chart, a long document, a bug fix and sorting files. Build the baseline first (`konrad-dev rebuild` on `origin/main`, then `podman tag konrad:local konrad:ab-a`), then the change. It needs a provider key; in unattended runs the capped one ([below](#a-real-model-in-unattended-runs)), with `anthropic/claude-haiku-5-5` at `--variant low` (the default) as a stand-in for the recommended local model. How fair a stand-in it is was measured once, against Qwen3.8 27B via OpenRouter on all the tasks ([report](tests/ab/reports/2026-10-29-models/)): 27B passed the graders' checks as often, but the blind judge preferred Haiku in 7 of 17 tasks and 27B in one, and 27B took six times as long, answered German input in English and once leaked a tool-call tag into its reply. So Haiku is a kind stand-in, hiding the polish, speed and language problems of a mid-size open-weights model: read a Haiku result as an upper bound, and check a change aimed at smaller models (instruction wording, language, "leave X out" rules) on one as well. For a skill change Haiku is no stand-in at all: unprompted it loads a skill in 0–2 of 10 runs, while 27B loads the matching one every time, and `--prompt-suffix` measures a skill's content in a setting no user is in ([ROADMAP → Lived with](ROADMAP.md#lived-with)). A fast small model and a local runtime weren't measured; the maintainer closed the question there (2026-10-29). To compare two models instead, give both sides the same image and each its own model: `--a-model`, `--b-model`, and `--a-variant`/`--b-variant` for the effort (`''` is the model's default). Podman only.
- `./scripts/ab-judge.sh blind|report <results>` — the blind judge on top: how good the deliverables are, beyond the graders' pass/fail checks. `blind` turns each pair of runs into two packets (X and Y swapped, under random ids) holding the task, its input and both deliverables as page renders, text and speaker notes (emails with their attachments, images, code), plus a list of the files each run left, and puts them in batches of ten, one task and one order per batch, each in a folder of its own with `JUDGE.md`. The agent session that ran the A/B hands each batch's folder to an [`ab-judge`](.claude/agents/ab-judge.md) subagent as the only path it gets: Sonnet, with only Read, Write and Glob, a start of about 17k tokens instead of a general-purpose subagent's 40k, which each judge pays again on every step and which made up more than half of what judging cost. Sonnet, not Opus: on the 2026-10-29 skills test Opus judges agreed with themselves more often (32 of 35 pairs) but cost about $0.20 a packet against Sonnet's $0.05. Each judge writes a `verdict.json` per packet without learning which side is which. The folder holding the batches can't be listed, so a judge's wildcard reaches only its own packets: in the first model comparison, four of 34 judges had read other packets' files through one, against the instruction not to. The list of batch folders, `judge-batches.txt`, sits beside the key in the results dir, so a judge that wanders up from its folder finds no other batch's name. `report` unblinds them, counts a pair for a side only when both orders agree, and writes `report/`: a dated `README.md` that reads like a short study (the answer and an overview first, then numbered sections: what was compared, how, results per task, limits), with side-by-side page images in `img/` only where one version won. Pick those pages yourself after reading the reasons, `--show <task>:<run>:<page>[,<page>]` per task, so each image shows what decided it, and name the sides (`--a-name Haiku --b-name "Qwen 27B"`) so the report doesn't speak of A and B. Commit it in the MR as `tests/ab/reports/<date>-<name>/` and link it from the description; GitLab and the GitHub mirror both display it, and it's public once merged ([the first one](tests/ab/reports/2026-10-28-office-skills/)). The judge found what the graders couldn't: in its first trial (2026-10-28) the deck without `powerpoint` won 10 of 10 pairs, on layout alone.
- `./scripts/smoke-test.sh konrad:local` — does the image have the right binaries / Python deps / baked content, and does the docling round-trip work? CI runs this same script. (Engine-agnostic and deliberately `bin/konrad`-free — CI runs it under Docker, and it validates the *image artifact*, not the host CLI.)
- `./scripts/selftest.sh` — the realistic end-to-end loop, and the right gate to hand an agent: it runs the smoke test, then drives a real `konrad run` *through `bin/konrad`* (uid mapping, workspace mount, config compose — the path a user actually takes) and asserts the agent answers. The **model comes from your own `~/.config/konrad` config** (override with `--model <slug>` / `KONRAD_SELFTEST_MODEL`, any provider; `--variant <effort>` / `KONRAD_SELFTEST_VARIANT` sets its reasoning effort); with no usable model/credential the model stage degrades to a SKIP, so a red result always means the *runtime* broke. One-time on your host: populate the shared `konrad-secrets` volume via `konrad-dev connect`. In `konrad code` and other unattended runs, use a capped test key instead ([below](#a-real-model-in-unattended-runs)). Not a CI gate.
- A live poke: `cd /tmp/konrad-test && konrad-dev --version` then `konrad-dev shell` to look around. Dump the full build manifest with `podman run --rm --entrypoint cat konrad:local /etc/konrad/build-manifest.json | jq .`.

**Always smoke-test locally before pushing changes that touch `image/`, `scripts/smoke-test.sh`, or `image/build-manifest.sh`.** CI catches the bug eventually but at a ~10 min round-trip cost per iteration vs. ~5.5 min locally (rebuild + smoke).

### A real model in unattended runs

An agent in `konrad code` runs the selftest's model stage when its session holds a provider key, and SKIPs it otherwise. Its box has open internet and the agent can read the key, so the key is made safe by what it can spend, not by being hidden ([ARCHITECTURE → konrad code](ARCHITECTURE.md#konrad-code)):

1. **Create a key just for this, with a hard spend limit**, never your everyday key. In the Anthropic Console, that's a workspace of its own (say `konrad-selftest`) with a low monthly spend limit, and an API key created inside that workspace: the limit belongs to the workspace, so a key in your Default workspace would share your normal budget. An OpenRouter key with a credit limit works the same way. Rotate it now and then.
2. **Connect it in each session that should use it.** Every `konrad code` session keeps its own nested volumes, so its own key store: the primary session, each parallel one (`s2`, …) and the `up` container. The key stays across restarts of that session. Pick the provider's API-key login (not a Pro/Max subscription login), and type the key only into that prompt, never into an agent's chat, whose transcript would keep it.
   - A terminal session: `konrad code --shell --session <name> https://gitlab.git.nrw/jbauss2/konrad` (the clone's session is `primary`), then `bin/konrad connect -p anthropic`.
   - The `up` container that serves sessions from the Claude app or claude.ai/code: from the host, find its `konrad-up-…` name with `podman ps --format '{{.Names}}'` (Linux) or `container ls` (macOS), then run the matching command below. A shell opened with `exec` doesn't inherit the entrypoint's `CONTAINERS_CONF_OVERRIDE`, and without it the key lands in the primary session's store.

   ```sh
   podman exec -it -u node -e CONTAINERS_CONF_OVERRIDE=/tmp/konrad-session-containers.conf -w /workspace/konrad <konrad-up-name> bin/konrad connect -p anthropic
   ```

   ```sh
   container exec -it -u node -e CONTAINERS_CONF_OVERRIDE=/tmp/konrad-session-containers.conf -w /workspace/konrad <konrad-up-name> bin/konrad connect -p anthropic
   ```

3. **Run the selftest with a cheap model at its lowest effort:** `./scripts/selftest.sh --model anthropic/claude-haiku-5-5 --variant low` after `konrad-dev rebuild` (add `--image konrad:latest` to test the released image instead). opencode lists a provider's models only once it's connected: `konrad-dev --profile selftest opencode models anthropic` shows them, and `--verbose` adds each model's variants.

## Commit style

[Conventional Commits 1.0.0](https://www.conventionalcommits.org/en/v1.0.0/), applied fully — by discipline, checked at review. CI reads them: the types pick the [version bump](#versioning), and every `feat`, `fix` and `perf` commit becomes a [CHANGELOG.md](CHANGELOG.md) entry: its subject, then the first paragraph of its body.

```text
type(scope)?: imperative, lowercase subject, no trailing period

First body paragraph — for feat, fix and perf: what changes for the user,
in plain words. It becomes the release note.

The rest of the body — for reviewers, expected for anything that needed a
design decision: explain *why* (surprising constraints, non-obvious
tradeoffs, measurements, links), wrapped at ~72 cols. Don't restate the
diff; the git log is the project's primary design history.

BREAKING CHANGE: <what breaks + how to migrate>   (footer, when applicable)
Co-Authored-By: ...                               (when applicable)
```

**Types** — `feat` (new capability), `fix` (bug fix), `docs`, `refactor` (no behaviour change), `perf`, `test`, `build` (build system / deps), `ci`, `style` (formatting only), `chore` (housekeeping — locks, etc.), `revert`.

**Scope** — optional; use one where it adds signal, from: `cli`, `image`, `config`, `skills`, `ci`, `locks`, `roadmap`, `release`.

**Breaking changes** — mark with `!` after the type/scope (e.g. `feat!:`) and/or a `BREAKING CHANGE:` footer. It makes the next release at least a **minor** bump — see [Versioning](#versioning).

**Release notes are the commits** — a `feat`, `fix` or `perf` commit's subject and first body paragraph are what users read in the release, so write them for users:

1. **The subject** says what a user can now do or what no longer goes wrong (`fix(cli): resume an apple/container pull that the registry cuts off`), not the function you changed.
2. **The body's first paragraph** says what changes for them, in plain words: no internals, no file or function names unless the user types them. For 0.42.1's first fix that would have been "When you told the agent what to call a file, it sometimes saved it in its own hidden working folder instead of where you'd look. It now saves it where you asked." rather than opening with how the agent prompt contradicted itself. A commit without a body gets its subject alone.
3. **Everything after that paragraph** is for reviewers and stays out of the notes: rationale, measurements, links, upstream issues, as detailed as the change needs.
4. **A fix users never saw** (to a test, a script, an unreleased feature) is `test`, `chore` or `refactor`, or folds into the commit it fixes.

`scripts/release.sh --preview` prints the notes a branch would release; the [MR template](.gitlab/merge_request_templates/Default.md) has a section for them, so they're read with the diff. The format (subject in bold, its first letter upper-cased unless it starts with `konrad`, the paragraph joined onto one line) is [cliff.toml](cliff.toml)'s.

**Release commit** — CI makes it: `chore(release): <version>`, bumping `VERSION` and adding `## [<version>] - <YYYY-MM-DD>` to CHANGELOG.md, through an auto-merging MR after every merge that has something to release ([Git tags & releases](#git-tags--releases)). Feature MRs never touch either file. A release that needs more than its commits say (a migration note, say) gets it from a maintainer edit to the release MR before it merges, or to CHANGELOG.md after.

## When to update what

**ROADMAP.md** — at most ten items: what automates the maintainer's checks, what keeps konrad safe and working for the maintainer's and their team's use, and what makes it smaller. An item comes in only when the maintainer wants it, and replaces an old one; an idea that doesn't make the cut lives in the commit or MR that raised it. A decision we made and are sticking with doesn't go there either (the commit message is enough). When an item ships, delete its bullet in the same commit. Outside the cap, **Upstream workarounds and limitations** tracks every upstream bug konrad works around or lives with: a commit that adds a workaround, or documents a limitation instead, adds its bullet there (upstream link, what to check, what to remove), and the commit that removes it deletes the bullet.

**CHANGELOG.md** — written by CI in the release commit, one entry per `feat`, `fix` and `perf` commit since the last release: its subject and the first paragraph of its body ([Keep a Changelog](https://keepachangelog.com/); the rationale after that paragraph stays in the commit). Feature MRs leave it alone.

**README.md** — anything that changes how a user installs, runs, or thinks about konrad. A new subcommand or flag. A new external dependency (e.g. a tool the user has to install on the host).

**CLAUDE.md** — this is the repo-level instructions file, loaded by Claude Code (and any other agent) working *on* konrad. Update when there's a new tool/file/directory the agent should know about, a new convention or constraint the agent should follow, or a structural change (config layering, state tiers, image stages). The runtime konrad agent's *environment manifest* lives separately at `image/opencode/instructions/environment.md` (baked into the image, loaded by opencode at runtime via the layered `instructions` globs — it's the baked layer's `instructions/` entry); update that file when shipped tools, Python libraries, or the filesystem layout change.

Keep all three tight — every byte competes with task context inside the model's window.
